label: 3 John 1:1–4
text:
"Prosper" is euodousthai, literally "to have a good road" (eu, "well," plus hodos, "way, journey") — an ordinary travel-metaphor stretched to cover overall well-being, "may your road go smoothly."

"Be in health" is hygiainein, the standard word for bodily soundness, the direct ancestor of English "hygiene."

"Even as thy soul prospereth" fixes the measure of the wish rather than merely adding to it — physical and material welfare is prayed for to the same degree spiritual welfare already stands, not beyond it.

"Testified" is martyrountōn, formal witness-bearing vocabulary — traveling believers arrive and give sworn, public testimony to Gaius's character, not passing gossip.
translation: The elder, to Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth. Beloved, I am praying concerning all things, that you may prosper and be in health, just as your soul is prospering. For I rejoiced exceedingly when the brothers came and testified to your truth, just as you are walking in truth. I have no greater joy than this: that I hear of my children walking in truth.

label: 3 John 1:5–8
text:
"Faithfully" translates piston, an adjective used adverbially — describing hospitality that is reliable, trustworthy, the same quality of dependability the word describes when applied to God's own promises elsewhere.

"Bring forward on their journey" is propempsas, a technical term for equipping and escorting travelers — providing supplies, guides, and expenses, the concrete, practical form early Christian hospitality to traveling missionaries actually took.

"After a godly sort" (axiōs tou theou) sets the standard for that support at the highest possible level — done in a manner actually worthy of God, not merely adequate.

"Taking nothing of the Gentiles" describes missionaries refusing pagan patronage specifically to avoid any appearance that the gospel depended on, or was beholden to, outside money — making the church's own support, described here, not optional generosity but the only legitimate source left.

"Fellowhelpers" is synergoi, "co-workers" — the identical term Paul regularly applies to his own ministry partners, extending full partnership in gospel work to those who only ever provide support from home.
translation: Beloved, you are doing a faithful work in whatever you do for the brothers, and these strangers, who have testified to your love before the church; whom you will do well to send forward on their journey in a manner worthy of God. Because for the sake of the name they went out, taking nothing from the Gentiles. We, then, ought to support such men, so that we may become fellow workers with the truth.

label: 3 John 1:9–11
text:
"Loveth to have the preeminence" translates philoprōteuōn, a rare compound apparently coined for this very occasion, fusing "loving" onto "being first" — a vivid character sketch of naked ambition condensed into a single word.

"Prating against" is phlyarōn, "to babble, to talk nonsense" — a dismissive, almost contemptuous verb for baseless chatter rather than substantive charges.

"Casteth...out" is ekballei, present tense — the same verb used elsewhere of driving out demons, here applied, with evident shock, to a man expelling fellow believers from their own congregation.

"Hath not seen God" is a perfect tense, ouch heōraken — a settled state of never having genuinely seen, and still not seeing, standing as the flat verdict John renders on evil conduct of exactly this kind.
translation: I wrote something to the church, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, does not receive us. Because of this, if I come, I will call to remembrance his works which he is doing, babbling against us with evil words; and not being content with these, neither does he himself receive the brothers, and he forbids those wanting to, and casts them out of the church. Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one doing good is of God; the one doing evil has not seen God.

label: 3 John 1:12–14
text:
"Hath good report" is memartyrētai, perfect passive — a reputation already well-established through testimony and, in the present, still standing firm, not a fresh or provisional impression.

"Ink and pen" (melanos kai kalamou) specifies kalamos, a reed used as a writing instrument, distinct from the sheet of papyrus named separately in the parallel closing of 2 John — the same farewell formula, dressed in slightly different vocabulary.

"Face to face" repeats the identical idiom, stoma pros stoma, "mouth to mouth," already used at the close of 2 John — John reaches for the same preference, direct speech over written correspondence, to end both short letters.

"By name" is kat' onoma, "according to name" — a deliberately individual greeting, each friend named and addressed personally rather than folded into a single collective blessing.
translation: Demetrius has been well testified of by all, and by the truth itself; and we also are testifying, and you know that our testimony is true. I was having many things to write to you, but I do not wish to write to you with ink and pen; but I am hoping to see you shortly, and we will speak mouth to mouth. Peace to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name.
